{{Short description|English humanist writer and mathematician}}
{{Use British English|date=August 2014}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2026}}
'''Thomas Blundeville''' (c. 1522 – c. 1606) was an English [[humanism|humanist]] writer and mathematician. He is known for work on [[logic]], [[astronomy]], education and [[horsemanship]], as well as for translations from the Italian. His interests were both wide-ranging and directed towards practical ends, and he adapted freely a number of the works he translated.

He was a pioneer writer in English in several areas, and inventor of a standard classroom geometrical instrument, the [[protractor]].

==Life==
He lived as a country gentleman on his estate at [[Newton Flotman]], in [[Norfolk]]. He inherited from his father Edward Blundeville in 1568, having possibly studied at the [[University of Cambridge]].<ref name = DNB>{{cite DNB|wstitle=Blundeville, Thomas (fl.1561)|volume=5}}</ref>

He had connections with court circles, and London scientific intellectuals. He was an associate of [[Henry Briggs (mathematician)|Henry Briggs]], at [[Gresham College]], and enjoyed the patronage of [[Robert Dudley, 1st Earl of Leicester]], among other aristocrats.<ref name = Hill>[[Christopher Hill (historian)|Christopher Hill]], ''Intellectual Origins of the English Revolution, Revisited'' (1997), p. 36.</ref>

Other indications on his life are more tenuous. It has been plausibly suggested that as "T. B." he added a prefatory poem to [[John Studley]]'s ''Agamemnon'';<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Valls-Russell | first = Janice
 | date = March 2020
 | doi = 10.3366/tal.2020.0407
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Translation and Literature
 | pages = 25–43
 | publisher = Edinburgh University Press
 | title = 'Even Seneca hymselfe to speke in englysh': John Studley's Hippolytus and Agamemnon
 | volume = 29}}</ref> he was certainly alluded to by [[Jasper Heywood]], in the preface to his ''Thyestes'' of 1560, as a translator of Plutarch.<ref name = DNB/> From this it is argued that he had connection to the [[Inns of Court]]. He may have travelled to Italy, an inference from his familiarity with Italian literature. He was a mathematics tutor, to households including that of [[Nicholas Bacon (courtier)|Nicholas Bacon]] and [[Francis Wyndham (judge)|Francis Wyndham]]; and Cecil may have recommended Blundeville to Leicester.<ref>Henry S. Turner, ''The English Renaissance Stage: Geometry, Poetics, and the Practical Spatial Arts 1580&ndash;1630'' (2006), pp. 56&ndash;7.</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Katherine Neal |journal=History of Science |year=1999 |volume=xxxvii |url=http://www.shpltd.co.uk/neal-rhetoric.pdf |title=The Rhetoric of Utility: Avoiding Occult Associations for Mathematics Through Profitability and Pleasure |access-date=2006-10-27 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080528234717/http://www.shpltd.co.uk/neal-rhetoric.pdf |archive-date=28 May 2008 }}, reading Francis Wyndham, dedicatee of ''Briefe Description of Universal Mappes'' per the DNB, for "Justice Windham".</ref> [[W. W. Rouse Ball]] gives a date of death of 1595, and possible connections to mathematicians: "Thomas Blundeville was resident at Cambridge about the same time as [[John Dee|Dee]] and [[Thomas Digges|Digges]]—possibly he was a non-collegiate student, and if so must have been one of the last of them."<ref name = Rouse>W. W. Rouse Ball, ''A history of the study of mathematics at Cambridge'' (1889), pp. 21&ndash;2, [https://archive.org/stream/historyofstudyof00balluoft/historyofstudyof00balluoft_djvu.txt online text].</ref>

He married twice, and his male heir Andrew was killed in the Flemish wars.<ref name = DNB/> His daughter Elizabeth married Rowland Meyrick, son of [[Sir Gelli Meyrick]] who was steward to [[Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex]] and caught up in his fall.<ref>John Burke, ''A Genealogical and Heraldic History of the Commoners of Great Britain and Ireland'' (1836), p. 634.</ref>

==Writings==

===Early works===
He made a partial verse translation of the ''Moralia'' of [[Plutarch]], to which [[Roger Ascham]] added verses.<ref>Lawrence V. Ryan, ''Roger Ascham'' (1963), p. 243.</ref> It appeared as ''Three Moral Treatises'' in 1561, his first work, to mark the accession of [[Elizabeth I]], to whom one of the pieces was dedicated. Another was dedicated to the courtiers [[John Harington (treasurer)|John Harington]] and [[John Astley (courtier)|John Astley]].<ref>http://www.thefreelibrary.com/Print,+patronage,+and+occasion:+translations+of+Plutarch%27s+Moralia+in...-a0181673908 ''Print, patronage, and occasion: translations of Plutarch's Moralia in Tudor England''</ref>

His book on horsemanship, ''The arte of ryding and breakinge greate horses'', was published about 1560 and is the first work on [[equitation]] published in English. It is an abridged and adapted translation, made at the suggestion of John Astley, of ''Gli ordini di cavalcare'' by [[Federico Grisone]], and is directed towards the use of horses in war.<ref>Joan Thirsk, ''The Rural Economy of England: Collected Essays'' (1980), p. 390.</ref><ref>Mary Augusta Scott, ''Elizabethan Translations from the Italian'' (1969), pp. 304&ndash;5.</ref> He followed it with ''The fower chiefyst offices belonging to Horsemanshippe'' (1565&ndash;6), which included a revised translation of Grisone together with other treatises.<ref name=fower>{{cite book|last=Blundeville|first=Thomas|title=The fower chiefyst offices belongyng to Horsemanshippe, That is to saye. The office of the Breeder, Of the Rider, of the Keper, and of the Ferrer ... Whyche bookes are not onely paynfully collected out of a nomber of aucthours, but also orderly dysposed and applyed to the vse of this oure coūtrey. By T. Blundeuill. (The Arte of Rydynge. Newly corrected and amended of many faultes escaped in the first Pryntynge ... through the dilygence of the first Author T. Blundeuill. – The Order of Dietynge of Horses, etc. – The Order of Curing Horses Diseases ... With the true art of paring & shooing al maner of houes, etc.)|year=1565|publisher=William Seres|location=London}}</ref> It was praised as "Xenophontean" by [[Gabriel Harvey]].<ref>[http://www.oxford-shakespeare.com/new_files_dec_21/Pierces_Supererogation.pdf ''Pierce's Supererogation, or A New Praise of the Old Ass.''(PDF)], at p. 29.</ref>

===Historiography===
His expressed views on history are considered standard for Elizabethan England.<ref>E.g. http://www.philological.bham.ac.uk/Nero/intro.html at note 10.</ref> The approach is causal, invoking the "meanes and instrumentes" of history, and mechanism in politics.<ref>Jessica Wolfe, ''Humanism, Machinery, and Renaissance Literature'' (2004), pp. 3&ndash;4.</ref> Influentially, he compromised between "linear" (traditional Christian medieval) and "cyclic" (classical) overall views of the working-out of history, for a "spiral" model. For him, the providential is not incompatible with the moral order as it asserts itself in the details of exemplary political history, and he has been compared to [[Edmund Bolton]] in combining the medieval and humanist traditions.<ref>Ivo Kamps, ''Historiography and Ideology in Stuart Drama'' (1996), p. 33 and p. 35.</ref><ref>Irving Ribner, ''The English History Play in the Age of Shakespeare'' (2005), p. 22.</ref> He commented that to be a good historiographer is a prerequisite for a counsellor, in his 1570 book on [[counsel]].<ref>[[Quentin Skinner]], ''Reason and Rhetoric in the Philosophy of Hobbes'' (1996), p. 82.</ref>

His ''True Order and Methode'' was dedicated to the Earl of Leicester and was a loose translation and summary of historiographical works by [[Jacopo Aconcio]] and [[Francesco Patrizzi]]. It endorsed the realist writing of history as process, and was one of the few English contributions of the period to the ''[[artes historicae]]''.<ref>Fritz Levy, ''Francis Bacon, The Advancement of Learning, and Historical Thought'', pp. 204&ndash;5 in Julie Robin Solomon, Catherine Gimelli Martin (editors), ''Francis Bacon and the Refiguring of Early Modern Thought: Essays to Commemorate The Advancement of Learning (1605&ndash;2005)'' (2005).</ref><ref>D. R. Woolf, ''The Shapes of History'',  p. 193 in David Scott Kastan (editor), ''A Companion to Shakespeare'' (1993).</ref> He translated also a manuscript of Aconcio on [[fortification]], for the [[Francis Russell, 2nd Earl of Bedford|Earl of Bedford]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.mhs.ox.ac.uk/staff/saj/aconcio/ | title=Jacopo Aconcio's lost treatise on fortification}}</ref>

===Logic===
His ''Arte of Logike'' (written 1575, published 1599) is somewhat [[Ramist]] in approach, but strongly so in discussing method.<ref>[http://e-research.tnstate.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1000&context=llp_wp Harry Maddux, ''The Virtuoso and Puritanism in 1676'' (PDF).], p. 10.</ref> Besides [[Aristotle]], it also shows the influence of [[Galen]], [[Melanchthon]], [[Cornelius Valerius]] the ''De Methodo'' of Aconcio of 1558, and [[Thomas Wilson (rhetorician)|Thomas Wilson]].<ref name = Pyle>[[Andrew Pyle (philosopher)|Andrew Pyle]] (editor), ''Dictionary of Seventeenth-Century British Philosophers'' (2000), article ''Blundeville, Thomas'', pp. 102&ndash;3.</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Blundeville |first1=Thomas |title=The Arte of Logike |date=1599 |page=66}}</ref>

It contains a section on [[fallacies]]. Under ''[[petitio principii]]'', it uses an even-handed example of [[Aristotelianism|Aristotelian]] and [[Copernican principle|Copernican]] arguments on the motion of the Earth.<ref>http://www.johndee.org/calder/html/Notes5.html, at note 60.</ref>

===Scientific, mathematical and geographical===
These later works are directed towards geography, [[navigation]] and travel, geography in Blundeville's view being a necessary support to history; their content is very mixed.<ref>Constance Caroline Relihan, ''Cosmographical Glasses: Geographic Discourse, Gender, and Elizabethan Fiction'' (2004), pp. 1&ndash;2.</ref>
[[File:Blundeville's Exercises on Cosmophraphy, Astronomy, etc. 1613 Edition.jpg|thumb|Blundeville's Exercises containing eight treatises including Cosmography, Astronomy, Geography and Navigation. Printed by Stansby, 1613.]]
The ''Exercises'' (1594) collected six treatises on practical skills, with a serious effort to be up-to-date. One of the parts described the world map of [[Petrus Plancius]], published two years earlier. Other topical matters covered were [[Emery Molyneux|Molyneux's globes]], the work of [[John Blagrave]] and [[Gemma Frisius]], and the [[cross-staff]] of [[Thomas Hood (mathematician)|Thomas Hood]].<ref>Willem Hackmann, ''Mathematical Instruments'', pp. 63&ndash;4 in John Fauvel, [[Raymond Flood (mathematician)|Raymond Flood]], [[Robin Wilson (mathematician)|Robin J. Wilson]] (editors), ''Oxford Figures: 800 Years of the Mathematical Sciences''.</ref> According to Rouse Ball:

{{cquote|In 1594 he published his Exercises in six parts, containing a brief account of arithmetic, cosmography, the use of the globes, a universal map, the astrolabe, and navigation. The arithmetic is taken from [[Robert Recorde|Recorde]], but to it are added trigonometrical tables (copied from [[Clavius]]) of the natural sines, tangents, and secants of all angles in the first quadrant; the difference between consecutive angles being one minute. These are worked out to seven places of decimals. This is the earliest English work in which plane trigonometry is introduced.<ref name = Rouse/>}}

A later edition (1613) showed the circumnavigations of [[Francis Drake]] and [[Thomas Cavendish]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.loc.gov/rr/rarebook/catalog/drake/drake-4-famousvoy.html |title = THE FAMOUS VOYAGE THE CIRCUMNAVIGATION OF THE WORLD 1577-1580: Sir Francis Drake: A Pictorial Biography by Hans P. Kraus (Rare Book and Special Collections Reading Room, Library of Congress)| website=[[Library of Congress]] }}</ref>

He collaborated on an astronomy book, ''The Theoriques of the Seuen Planets'' (1602), assisted by [[Lancelot Browne]] as he notes in the preface.<ref>Mordechai Feingold, ''The Mathematicians' Apprenticeship: Science, Universities and Society in England, 1560&ndash;1640'' (1984), p. 50.</ref> It contained also information about the recent research of [[William Gilbert (astronomer)|William Gilbert]] on the Earth's magnetic field, which he included with help from [[Edward Wright (mathematician)|Edward Wright]] and Henry Briggs. Wright had earlier supplied some of the innovative material for his writing on [[navigation]] in the ''Exercises''. He had worked with [[William Barlow (archdeacon)|William Barlow]] and others on the required scientific instruments; according to Hill Blundeville invented the protractor.<ref name = Hill/> In fact he described a semicircular instrument for measuring angles in 1589, in his ''Briefe Description of Universal Mappes and Cardes''.<ref>Amy Ackerberg-Hastings, ''Protractors in the Classroom: An Historical Perspective'', p. 217 in [[Amy Shell-Gellasch]], Dick Jardine (editors), ''From Calculus to Computers: Using the Last 200 Years of Mathematics History in the Classroom'' (2005).</ref>
